introduction-batch-vs-service.core: Services (web apps) run forever and must stay available; batch jobs (training, simulations) run to completion and want maximum resources for a period. Slurm is a batch scheduler built to queue jobs and pack them fairly onto large clusters, especially multi-node GPU jobs.

first_principles.problem: A team runs week-long multi-node training on a scheduler designed for always-on services.
truths: Batch jobs have a start and end.
Large jobs need all their nodes at once (gang scheduling).
Queues let demand exceed supply fairly.

analogy.title: A restaurant kitchen versus a factory batch line
analogy.story: The kitchen serves continuous orders; the factory runs scheduled production batches.
analogy.breaks: Factories don't backfill other products into idle machines minute by minute; Slurm does.

check.q: Why does multi-node training need gang scheduling?
check.a: All ranks must start together; partial allocation would hold resources idle waiting for the rest.

slurm-architecture-the-controller-and-th.core: slurmctld is the central controller that tracks nodes, queues and scheduling decisions; slurmd runs on every compute node to launch and monitor job steps; slurmdbd stores accounting in a database for fair-share and reporting. Users submit from login nodes.

first_principles.problem: A job is stuck 'PD' and the user doesn't know which component to ask.
derivation: **slurmctld**: state and scheduling (with a backup controller).

analogy.title: An air-traffic control tower and ground crews
analogy.story: The tower schedules all take-offs; each gate's crew handles its plane.
analogy.breaks: A tower failure grounds everything, which is why Slurm runs a backup controller.

example.title: Why is my job pending?

steps.label: Finding
steps.detail: Reason=Priority: other users have higher fair-share.

code.text:
squeue -u $USER -o '%i %T %r'
scontrol show job 12345 | grep Reason

example.outcome: state understood from the right component.

check.a: A database of job accounting used for fair-share priority and usage reporting.

the-language-of-slurm-sbatch.core: An sbatch script is a bash script with #SBATCH comment directives declaring resources (nodes, tasks, GPUs, memory, time, partition). sbatch queues it and returns a job ID; output goes to files, and environment variables like SLURM_JOB_ID describe the allocation.

first_principles.problem: Users run long jobs interactively on login nodes and lose them when SSH drops.
truths: Jobs must declare resources up front.

analogy.title: A work order submitted to the facilities team
analogy.story: You state what you need, how long and where, then they schedule it.
analogy.breaks: Facilities might extend a job; Slurm kills it at the time limit.

check.q: Why should you set a realistic --time?
check.a: The scheduler uses it to backfill jobs into gaps; overestimates delay your start, underestimates get the job killed.

resource-allocation-gres-tasks-and-srun.core: GRES (generic resources) lets Slurm schedule GPUs (--gres=gpu:8 or --gpus-per-node). Tasks map to processes (--ntasks-per-node, usually one per GPU). Inside an allocation, srun launches the job steps across nodes, setting rank variables used by distributed frameworks.

first_principles.problem: A multi-node PyTorch job starts with the wrong number of processes and ranks collide.
truths: One process per GPU is the common pattern.
Frameworks need rank and world size.

analogy.title: Booking hotel rooms and assigning guests
analogy.story: You book floors (nodes) and rooms (GPUs), then the concierge (srun) puts one guest in each room.
analogy.breaks: Guests choose their rooms; processes need explicit GPU binding.

code.text:
#SBATCH --nodes=4
#SBATCH --ntasks-per-node=8
#SBATCH --gpus-per-node=8
#SBATCH --cpus-per-task=12
export MASTER_ADDR=$(scontrol show hostnames $SLURM_NODELIST | head -1)
srun python train.py  # RANK=$SLURM_PROCID, WORLD_SIZE=$SLURM_NTASKS

check.q: Which variable usually gives a process its global rank under srun?

partitions-and-qos-the-traffic-lights.core: Partitions group nodes into queues with their own limits (e.g. gpu, cpu, debug). QOS (Quality of Service) sets per-job or per-user policy: max GPUs, max wall time and priority, plus whether a job can preempt others. Together with fair-share they decide who runs when.

first_principles.problem: One team's 500 queued jobs block everyone else's quick debug runs.
truths: Short jobs benefit from fast lanes.

analogy.title: Traffic lanes and lights
analogy.story: A bus lane, a fast lane with a speed limit and lights that let emergency vehicles through.
analogy.breaks: Traffic lights are fixed timers; fair-share adapts to recent usage.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Starts in minutes while big jobs queue on gpu.

check.q: What's the difference between a partition and a QOS?
check.a: A partition is a set of nodes forming a queue; a QOS is a policy (limits, priority, preemption) attached to jobs.

checkpointing-surviving-preemption-and-n.core: Long multi-node jobs will hit time limits, preemption or hardware failure. Save model, optimiser, scheduler, RNG and data-loader state regularly to shared storage, trap Slurm's warning signal (--signal) to save before kill, and requeue so the job resumes from the latest checkpoint.

first_principles.problem: A node dies at hour 40 of a 48-hour run with no checkpoint.
truths: At scale, failure probability per day is high.
Exact resume needs all state, not only weights.
derivation: Checkpoint **every N steps** to shared FS.
**--signal=USR1@300** to save before the time limit.
**--requeue** and resume from the latest checkpoint.

analogy.title: Saving a video game before the boss fight
analogy.story: If you lose, you restart from the save point, not the beginning.
analogy.breaks: A game save is instant; large checkpoints take minutes, so frequency trades overhead against lost work.

example.title: Signal-driven save

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Five minutes' warning to save, then the job requeues and resumes.

code.text:
#SBATCH --signal=B:USR1@300
#SBATCH --requeue
trap 'touch SAVE_NOW' USR1
srun python train.py --resume latest &
wait

example.outcome: at most minutes of work lost.

check.q: Why checkpoint optimizer state, not just weights?
check.a: Optimisers like Adam hold moment estimates; without them, resumed training behaves differently and can diverge.

slurm-vs-kubernetes-the-cage-match.core: Slurm excels at batch HPC: gang scheduling, fair-share, topology awareness and bare-metal performance. Kubernetes excels at services, containers, autoscaling and ecosystem. Many AI orgs use Slurm for big training and Kubernetes for serving, or bridge them (Slinky, Kueue, Volcano).

first_principles.problem: A team debates migrating a research cluster from Slurm to Kubernetes based on hype.
derivation: **Bridge**: Kueue/Volcano for batch on K8s, or Slurm on K8s.
Decide by **workload mix and team skills**.

analogy.title: A freight railway versus a city bus network
analogy.story: Rail moves huge scheduled loads efficiently; buses serve continuous flexible routes.
analogy.breaks: Both systems keep borrowing each other's features, so the line keeps blurring.

check.q: What key batch feature does vanilla Kubernetes scheduling lack?
check.a: Gang scheduling: starting all pods of a job together (added by Kueue/Volcano).
